## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.50845.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.50845.sa1)

In the interests of transparency, eLife publishes the most substantive revision requests and the accompanying author responses.

Acceptance summary:

The manuscript builds on the authors recent study, in which they showed that a dopamine dehydroxylase (Dadh) from Eggerthella lenta degrades L-dopa, the precursor to the neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine. In this manuscript, the authors first explore the substrate specificity of the E. lenta enzyme in more detail and find that it is rather narrow. Dadh from E. lenta degrades dopamine and norepinephrine, but not epinephrine or other, more distantly related catecholamines. Importantly, only dopamine and norepinephrine induce expression of Dadh, with both substrates promoting E. lenta growth by serving as alternative electron acceptors. The authors then use similar reasoning as they used for identification of E. lenta Dadh to prospect for additional Dadh-related enzymes from Actinobacteria that might dehydroxylate other catechols. The authors identify such activities for three other catechols including DOPAC, catechin and hydrocaffeic acid in Gordonia pamelaeae and E. lenta. Bioinformatic analyses and activity assays with a variety of bacterial communities indicate that these catechol hydroxylases are widely distributed. For the revision, the authors added biochemical data that specifically link the hcdh gene to hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylation, and they provided additional data in support of the metabolic functions identified in low-abundance gut Actinobacteria being prevalent but variably distributed among human gut microbiotae. In aggregate, this work has important implications not only for the turnover of medical drugs in human and animal guts, but likely also for many other microbial ecosystems, since catechols comprise a widely distributed class of molecules.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "A widely distributed metalloenzyme class enables gut microbial metabolism of host-and diet-derived catechols" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by three peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Detlef Weigel as Reviewing and Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal her identity: Ruth Ley (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers and I have discussed the reviews, and I have drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

Summary:

The current work builds on your recent study, in which you showed that a dopamine dehydroxylase (Dadh) from Eggerthella lenta degrades L-dopa, the precursor to the neurotransmitters dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine. In the current work, you first explore the substrate specificity of the E. lenta enzyme in more detail and find that it is rather narrow. Dadh from E. lenta degrades dopamine and norepinephrine, but not epinephrine or other, more distantly related catecholamines. Importantly, only dopamine and norepinephrine induce expression of Dadh, with both substrates promoting E. lenta growth by serving as alternative electron acceptors.

You then use similar reasoning as you used for identification of E. lenta Dadh to prospect for additional Dadh-related enzymes from Actinobacteria that might dehydroxylate other catechols. You identify such activities for three other catechols including DOPAC, catechin and hydrocaffeic acid in Gordonia pamelaeae and E. lenta. Bioinformatic analyses and activity assays with a variety of bacterial communities indicate that these catechol hydroxylases are widely distributed. In aggregate, this work has important implications not only for the turnover of medical drugs in human and animal guts, but likely also for many other microbial ecosystems, since catechols comprise a widely distributed class of molecules.

Essential revisions:

The reviewers were all very positive, but also agreed that the work would be enhanced by more definitive data showing directly that at least one of the newly identified enzymes is responsible for the observed chemical transformations. This could come either from in vitro assays with purified protein or genetic assays. One of the major conclusions of the manuscript is that catechol dehydroxylation is performed by distinct subtypes of molybdenum-dependent enzymes, but this statement is only fully supported if you can unequivocally show that the identified enzymes perform the chemical transformation they suggested.

A more general suggestion is that the disparate nature of the data make for a somewhat disconnected presentation. We would strongly encourage you to think of ways to connect the different data sources more strongly. For example, given the isolate data, from generally low abundance Actinobacteria, how prevalent do you think these functions actually are in human guts? Your human gut data (Figure 2E) suggest that individuals can have log order differences in Dadh copy number and that some ex vivo communities are responsive to dopamine, while others are not. Why might this be? Are there other enzymes, such as those in the SSN, that might perform this function? In Figure 2—figure supplement 7, E. lenta counts do not increase in response to dopamine in all ex vivo samples – what might be behind this observation? The observed functional and metabolic diversity across human individuals is obviously fascinating and more could be done to discuss it in the context of the rest of the paper.

Notwithstanding these comments, there was general agreement that this is a fine example of the integrated use of different approaches to elucidate a previously mysterious metabolic activity of the gut microbiome (catechol dehydroxylation), both by discovering the family of enzymes responsible for it and demonstrating its apparent benefit for the encoding bacteria.

claims.source: Altogether, these results are consistent with the hypothesis that dopamine dehydroxylation can increase the fitness of metabolizing E. lenta strains in microbial communities.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competition and community experiments.

claims.claim: Among human gut bacteria, only Eggerthella and closely related members of the Actinobacteria phylum have been reported to perform catechol dehydroxylation.
claims.source: Among human gut bacteria, only Eggerthella and closely related members of the Actinobacteria phylum have been reported to perform catechol dehydroxylation. For example, Eggerthella metabolizes dopamine (Maini Rekdal et al., 2019) and (+)-catechin (Takagaki and Nanjo, 2015), while related Gordonibacter species dehydroxylate ellagic acid (Selma et al., 2014) and didemethylsecoisolariciresinol (dmSECO), an intermediate in the multi-step biosynthesis of the anti-cancer metabolite enterodiol (Bess et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Both DOPAC and hydrocaffeic acid are directly dehydroxylated by members of the gut Actinobacterial library.
claims.source: This analysis showed that both DOPAC and hydrocaffeic acid are directly dehydroxylated by members of this library, while (+)-catechin undergoes benzyl ether reduction followed by dehydroxylation into derivative 2, as has been observed previously (Takagaki and Nanjo, 2015) (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by LC-MS analysis of bacterial cultures.

claims.claim: The dehydroxylation of DOPAC and hydrocaffeic acid has only been previously observed by complex gut microbiota communities.
claims.source: While (+)-catechin metabolism has been previously linked to Eggerthella (Takagaki and Nanjo, 2015), the dehydroxylation of DOPAC and hydrocaffeic acid has only been previously observed by complex gut microbiota communities (Scheline et al., 1960; Peppercorn and Goldman, 1972).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to historical literature.

claims.claim: The variability in dehydroxylation activities across closely related gut bacterial strains suggests that distinct enzymes might dehydroxylate different catechols.
claims.source: The variability in these activities across closely related gut bacterial strains suggests that distinct enzymes might dehydroxylate different catechols.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed variability in metabolism across strains.

claims.claim: Dehydroxylation is an inducible activity in Gordonibacter and Eggerthella strains.
claims.source: To test the hypothesis specific rather than promiscuous enzymes were involved, we first established that dehydroxylation is an inducible activity in Gordonibacter and Eggerthella strains (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments showing oxygen sensitivity and inducibility of dehydroxylase activity.

claims.claim: Each E. lenta A2 lysate quantitively dehydroxylated only the catechol substrate with which the strain had been grown.
claims.source: Consistent with our prediction, each lysate quantitively dehydroxylated only the catechol substrate with which the strain had been grown. While the E. lenta lysates did not display any promiscuity (Figure 4A), cell lysate from G. pamelaeae grown in the presence of DOPAC displayed reduced activity (<45% conversion) towards hydrocaffeic acid, which structurally resembles DOPAC (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by lysate assays shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claims.claim: Different catechol substrates induce the expression of distinct dehydroxylase enzymes that are specific in their activity and transcriptional regulation.
claims.source: Overall, these results suggest that different catechol substrates induce the expression of distinct dehydroxylase enzymes that are specific in their activity and transcriptional regulation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lysate specificity experiments.

claims.claim: Hydrocaffeic acid and (+)-catechin each upregulated a number of genes in E. lenta A2, including two predicted molybdenum-dependent enzymes.
claims.source: Hydrocaffeic acid and (+)-catechin each upregulated a number of genes (21 and 43, respectively), including two predicted molybdenum-dependent enzymes (Supplementary files 2a and 2b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: The candidate hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylase (hcdh) shares 35.3% amino acid identity with Dadh.
claims.source: The candidate hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylase (Elenta-A2_02815, named hcdh) shares 35.3% amino acid identity with Dadh, while the candidate (+)-catechin dehydroxylase (E. lenta-A2_00577, named cadh) shares 50.9% amino acid identity with Dadh (Supplementary files 2a-2c).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claims.claim: Tungstate inhibited dehydroxylation of (+)-catechin and hydrocaffeic acid by E. lenta A2 without inhibiting growth.
claims.source: As with dopamine dehydroxylation, tungstate inhibited dehydroxylation of (+)-catechin and hydrocaffeic acid by E. lenta A2 without inhibiting growth in the rich BHI medium, suggesting these activities are indeed molybdenum dependent (Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments with tungstate shown in supplementary figures.

claims.claim: Tungstate did not inhibit benzyl ether reduction of (+)-catechin, indicating this step is likely performed by a distinct enzyme.
claims.source: Tungstate did not inhibit benzyl ether reduction of (+)-catechin, indicating this step is likely performed by a distinct enzyme (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments showing tungstate does not affect benzyl ether reduction.

claims.claim: The overall distribution of the genes encoding the putative hydrocaffeic acid and (+)-catechin dehydroxylating enzymes across closely related Eggerthella strains correlated with metabolism of each substrate.
claims.source: Finally, we found that the overall distribution of the genes encoding these the putative hydrocaffeic acid and (+)-catechin dehydroxylating enzymes across closely related Eggerthella strains correlated with metabolism of each substrate (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics and metabolism data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Eggerthella uses distinct molybdenum-dependent enzymes to dehydroxylate hydrocaffeic acid and (+)-catechin.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest that Eggerthella uses distinct molybdenum-dependent enzymes dehydroxylate hydrocaffeic acid and (+)-catechin.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNA-seq, tungstate inhibition, and comparative genomics data.

claims.claim: One molybdenum-dependent enzyme-encoding gene (C1877_13905) in G. pamelaeae 3C was among the highest upregulated genes in response to DOPAC in two independent RNA-seq experiments.
claims.source: One of these genes (C1877_13905) was among the highest upregulated genes across the dataset (>1700 fold induced). To further explore the association between this gene and DOPAC dehydroxylation, we repeated the RNA-seq experiment, growing G. pamelaeae 3C in the presence of DOPAC from the time of inoculation and then harvesting cells in mid-exponential phase as soon we could detect metabolism (12 hr of growth). In this experiment, the same molybdenum-dependent enzyme-encoding gene (C1877_13905) that was highly upregulated in our first experiment (Supplementary file 2e) was among the highest upregulated genes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by two independent RNA-seq experiments.

claims.claim: Carriage of C1877_13905 (dodh) correlated with DOPAC dehydroxylation among members of the gut Actinobacterial library.
claims.source: This assignment is also supported by comparative genomics. First, carriage of C1877_13905 (named dodh) correlated with DOPAC dehydroxylation among members of our gut Actinobacterial library (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics and metabolism data.

claims.claim: The functionally annotated gene most similar to the candidate DOPAC dehydroxylase is Cldh, a Gordonibacter enzyme recently implicated in the dehydroxylation of dmSECO.
claims.source: Finally, the functionally annotated gene most similar to the candidate DOPAC dehydroxylase is Cldh (45% amino acid ID), a Gordonibacter enzyme recently implicated in the dehydroxylation of the lignan dmSECO (Bess et al., 2020) (Supplementary file 2c).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence similarity and a citation to a recent study.

claims.claim: Tungstate did not inhibit dehydroxylation of DOPAC by G. pamelaeae.
claims.source: Interestingly, unlike with the Eggerthella dehydroxylases, tungstate did not inhibit dehydroxylation of DOPAC by G. pamelaeae (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experiments with tungstate.

claims.claim: The lack of tungstate inhibition of DOPAC dehydroxylation may be explained if the dehydroxylating enzyme can use both molybdenum and tungsten for catalysis.
claims.source: This may be explained if the dehydroxylating enzyme can use both molybdenum and tungsten for catalysis, as is seen in certain closely related enzymes (Rosner and Schink, 1995).
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on analogy to other enzymes and supported by a citation.

claims.claim: An active fraction from E. lenta A2 containing the hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylase quantitatively dehydroxylated hydrocaffeic acid into m-hydroxyphenylacetic acid under anaerobic conditions.
claims.source: This yielded an active fraction that contained five major bands as assessed by SDS-PAGE (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) and quantitatively dehydroxylated hydrocaffeic acid into m-hydroxyphenylacetic acid under anaerobic conditions (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enzyme assays shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Proteomics confirmed that the band with the apparent correct size contained the proposed hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylase (Hcdh).
claims.source: We confirmed that the band with the apparent correct size (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) contained the proposed hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylase (Hcdh, Elenta-A2_02815) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5 and Supplementary file 2f) using proteomics.
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data.

claims.claim: The partially purified Hcdh preparation dehydroxylated only hydrocaffeic acid and not dopamine, (+)-catechin, or DOPAC.
claims.source: Consistent with our experiments in cell lysates (Figure 4A), we observed dehydroxylation only of hydrocaffeic acid and not of dopamine, (+)-catechin, or DOPAC (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by enzyme assays shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The putative catechol dehydroxylases from E. lenta and G. pamelaeae differ in sequence identity, genomic context, and predicted subunit composition.
claims.source: Despite being expected to perform the same type of chemical reaction, the putative catechol dehydroxylases from E. lenta and G. pamelaeae differ in sequence identity, genomic context, and predicted subunit composition (Supplementary file 3a and Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and genomic context analysis.

claims.claim: The dopamine, catechin and hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylases from E. lenta are likely membrane-bound complexes.
claims.source: The dopamine, catechin and hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylases from E. lenta (dadh, cadh and hcdh, respectively) are likely membrane-bound complexes as they co-localize with genes encoding an electron shuttling 4Fe-4S ferredoxin and a putative membrane anchor (Figure 4—figure supplement 6) (Rothery et al., 2008; Rothery and Weiner, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic context analysis and citations to literature on similar enzymes.

claims.claim: The E. lenta dehydroxylases carry a Twin-Arginine-Translocation (TAT) signal sequence, suggesting they are exported from the cytoplasm.
claims.source: These enzymes all carry a Twin-Arginine-Translocation (TAT) signal sequence, suggesting they are exported from the cytoplasm before the signal sequence is cleaved off.
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and knowledge of TAT signal sequences.

claims.claim: No peptide coverage of the TAT signal sequence was found in the proteomics experiment that identified E. lenta Hcdh, confirming that this sequence is cleaved in the mature protein.
claims.source: We found no peptide coverage of the TAT signal sequence in the proteomics experiment that identified E. lenta Hcdh, further confirming that this sequence is cleaved in the mature protein as in other membrane-anchored moco enzymes (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) (Iobbi-Nivol and Leimkühler, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by proteomics data and a citation.

claims.claim: The putative G. pamelaeae dehydroxylases do not harbor a TAT signal sequence, are smaller than the E. lenta enzymes, and are likely soluble protein complexes.
claims.source: In contrast, dodh and similar enzymes from G. pamelaeae do not harbor a TAT signal sequence, are smaller than the E. lenta enzymes, and co-localize with a gene predicted to encode a small electron shuttling 4Fe-4S protein, suggesting they are likely soluble protein complexes (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence and genomic context analysis.

claims.claim: The putative G. pamelaeae dehydroxylases are encoded adjacent to members of the Major Facilitator Superfamily, transporters that may import or export the catechol substrates or dehydroxylated metabolites.
claims.source: These putative G. pamelaeae dehydroxylases are also encoded adjacent to members of the Major Facilitator Superfamily, transporters that may import or export the catechol substrates or dehydroxylated metabolites (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic context analysis and speculation about transporter function.

claims.claim: There exist distinct subtypes of molybdenum-dependent catechol dehydroxylases.
claims.source: Altogether, these data indicate the existence of distinct subtypes of molybdenum-dependent catechol dehydroxylases.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differences in sequence, genomic context, and predicted structure.

claims.claim: Dadh and hcdh were the most prevalent catechol dehydroxylases in human gut metagenomes (in >70% and >90% of individuals, respectively).
claims.source: Dadh and hcdh were the most prevalent (in >70% and>90% of individuals, respectively), followed by cadh (30%), dodh (20%), and cldh (25%) (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of >1800 human gut metagenomes.

claims.claim: The prevalence of the different dehydroxylase genes in metagenomes is consistent with their distribution among individual human gut Actinobacterial isolates.
claims.source: Notably, the prevalence of the different genes in metagenomes is consistent with their distribution among individual human gut Actinobacterial isolates (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison between metagenomic data and strain-level data.

claims.claim: Dehydroxylation of dopamine, hydrocaffeic acid, and DOPAC was observed across the majority of human fecal samples cultured ex vivo.
claims.source: In this experiment, we observed dehydroxylation of dopamine, hydrocaffeic acid, and DOPAC across the majority of subjects, indicating that metabolic activities of low-abundance gut Actinobacteria are indeed prevalent (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex vivo culturing experiments with human fecal samples.

claims.claim: Catechol metabolism varied between compounds and subjects.
claims.source: However, catechol metabolism varied between compounds and subjects, with some individuals metabolizing all compounds and some metabolizing none (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the ex vivo culturing data.

claims.claim: The abundance of the candidate DOPAC dehydroxylase gene dodh discriminated metabolizing and non-metabolizing subjects.
claims.source: qPCR enumeration in these cultures revealed that the abundance of the candidate DOPAC dehydroxylase gene dodh discriminated metabolizing and nonmetabolizing subjects (p<0.001, unpaired t-test) (Figure 4E), and correlated significantly with dehydroxylation activity within the nine metabolizers (Pearson's correlation, r = 0.73, R2 = 0.53, p<0.05) (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qPCR data from ex vivo cultures.

claims.claim: Catechol dehydroxylases form a unique clade within the bis-MGD enzyme family, clustering away from pyrogallol hydroxytransferase (Pht).
claims.source: Further phylogenetic analysis revealed that catechol dehydroxylases form a unique clade within the bis-MGD enzyme family, clustering away from pyrogallol hydroxytransferase (Pht), the only other bis-MGD enzyme known to modify the aromatic ring of a substrate (Messerschmidt et al., 2004) (Figure 6 and Supplementary file 3b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: The catechol dehydroxylases are most closely related to acetylene hydratase.
claims.source: The catechol dehydroxylases are instead most closely related to acetylene hydratase, an enzyme that adds water to acetylene to provide a carbon source for the marine Proteobacterium Pelobacter acetylenicus (Figure 6) (Tenbrink et al., 2011; Rosner and Schink, 1995; Schoepp-Cothenet et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations.

claims.claim: A sequence similarity network (SSN) analysis revealed distinct clusters of catechol dehydroxylases.
claims.source: A sequence similarity network (SSN) analysis using sequences of bis-MGD enzymes revealed distinct clusters of catechol dehydroxylases, further suggesting these enzymes are functionally different from known family members (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by SSN analysis.

claims.claim: The clustering of the dehydroxylases in the SSN did not simply reflect the phylogeny of the organisms.
claims.source: The clustering of the dehydroxylases in the SSN did not simply reflect the phylogeny of the organisms because additional sequences from both Eggerthella and Gordonibacter were found in clusters containing distinct, biochemically characterized enzymes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the SSN.

claims.claim: Catechol dehydroxylases are a distinct group of molybdenum-dependent enzymes.
claims.source: Based on these data, we propose that catechol dehydroxylases are a distinct group of molybdenum-dependent enzymes.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from phylogenetic and SSN analyses.

claims.claim: Catechol dehydroxylases are not restricted to human-associated Actinobacteria and are present in diverse bacteria and even Archaea.
claims.source: Our analysis also revealed that catechol dehydroxylases are not restricted to human-associated Actinobacteria and are instead part of a larger group of bis-MGD enzymes present in diverse bacteria and even Archaea (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Notable organisms encoding putative dehydroxylases include soil-dwelling Streptomycetes, Clostridium ljungdahlii, and anaerobic bacterial genera known for their ability to degrade aromatic compounds.
claims.source: Notable organisms encoding putative dehydroxylases include soil-dwelling Streptomycetes (Wu et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2012), the industrially important anaerobe Clostridium ljungdahlii (Köpke et al., 2010), and a large number of anaerobic bacterial genera known for their ability to degrade aromatic compounds, including Azoarcus, Thauera, Desulfobacula, Geobacter, Desulfumonile, and Desulfitobacterium (Figure 7) (DeWeerd et al., 1991; Wöhlbrand et al., 2013; Butler et al., 2007; Wagner et al., 2012; Cole et al., 1995; Fernández et al., 2014; Molina-Fuentes et al., 2015; Villemur et al., 2006; Pacheco-Sánchez et al., 2019a).
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and citations to literature on these organisms.

claims.claim: The presence of similar enzymes in gut and environmental microbes likely reflects the availability of catechol substrates in many different environments.
claims.source: The presence of similar enzymes in gut and environmental microbes likely reflects the availability of catechol substrates in many different environments (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of dehydroxylases.

claims.claim: A putative dehydroxylase is present in Streptomyces biosynthetic gene clusters that produce yatakemycin and CC-1065.
claims.source: For instance, a putative dehydroxylase is present in Streptomyces biosynthetic gene clusters that produce the potent anti-tumor compounds yatakemycin and CC-1065 (Wu et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2012) (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claims.claim: Gene knock-out and complementation studies revealed a Streptomyces dehydroxylase homolog is essential for CC-1065 production and likely catalyzes reductive dehydroxylation of a late-stage biosynthetic intermediate.
claims.source: Gene knock-out and complementation studies revealed this enzyme is essential for CC-1065 production and likely catalyzes reductive dehydroxylation of a late-stage biosynthetic intermediate (Wu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to a genetic study.

claims.claim: A dehydroxylase homolog is present in the 3,5-dihydroxybenzoate (3,5-DHB) degradation operon within Thauera aromatica.
claims.source: Another homolog is present in the 3,5-dihydroxybenzoate (3,5-DHB) degradation operon within the anaerobic soil Proteobacterium Thaeura aromatica (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on genomic analysis.

claims.claim: Thauera aromatica strains lacking a dehydroxylase homolog exhibit impaired growth on 3,5-DHB as a sole carbon source.
claims.source: Strains lacking this enzyme exhibit impaired growth on 3,5-DHB as a sole carbon source, suggesting a possible role for this enzyme in metabolizing the one of the two catecholic intermediates involved in this pathway (Molina-Fuentes et al., 2015; Pacheco-Sánchez et al., 2019a; Pacheco-Sánchez et al., 2019b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies.

claims.claim: The catechol dehydroxylases harbor vast uncharacterized diversity that contributes to both primary and secondary metabolic pathways in habitats beyond the human gut.
claims.source: Based on this analysis, we conclude that the catechol dehydroxylases harbor vast uncharacterized diversity that contributes to both primary and secondary metabolic pathways in habitats beyond the human gut.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic analysis and genetic studies.

claims.claim: Catechol dehydroxylation was observed across the gut microbiotas of mammals spanning different diets and phylogenies.
claims.source: We observed catechol dehydroxylation across the gut microbiotas of mammals spanning different diets and phylogenies (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex vivo culturing experiments with mammalian fecal samples.

claims.claim: Hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylation occurred in >50% of mammalian species tested.
claims.source: Hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylation occurred in >50% of species, while dopamine and (+)-catechin metabolism were observed in 5/12 and 4/12 animals, respectively (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ex vivo culturing data shown in Figure 8.

claims.claim: DOPAC was only metabolized by the rat gut microbiota.
claims.source: DOPAC was only metabolized by the rat gut microbiota, which was the only community that had activity towards all compounds tested.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the ex vivo culturing data.

claims.claim: Catechol dehydroxylation is found in distantly related mammal gut microbiotas that have large differences in species composition and gene content.
claims.source: While a larger sample size is required to reach clear conclusions about possible links between metabolism of specific catechols and individual mammal gut microbiotas, our results clearly demonstrate that catechol dehydroxylation is found in distantly related mammal gut microbiotas that have large differences in species composition and gene content (Reese et al., 2018; Reese et al., 2019; Coelho et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mammalian ex vivo data and supported by citations.

claims.claim: The specificity of Dadh for dopamine suggested this metabolic activity might have an important physiological role in E. lenta.
claims.source: The specificity of Dadh for dopamine suggested this metabolic activity might have an important physiological role in E. lenta.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the substrate specificity data.

claims.claim: Dadh is the first catecholamine-metabolizing enzyme from a human gut commensal.
claims.source: To our knowledge, Dadh is the first catecholamine-metabolizing enzyme from a human gut commensal.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding.

claims.claim: Interactions between catecholamines and intestinal pathogens are well-characterized and have long been known as key players in virulence and infection.
claims.source: However, interactions between catecholamines and intestinal pathogens are well-characterized and have long been known as key players in virulence and infection (Freestone et al., 2007; Lyte and Ernst, 1992).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Pathogenic organisms such as E. coli, Y. enterocolitica, and S. enterica require the intact catechol group of dopamine and norepinephrine to sequester iron and boost growth.
claims.source: Whereas pathogenic organisms such as Escherichia coli, Yersinia enterocolitica, and Salmonella enterica require the intact catechol group of dopamine and norepinephrine to sequester iron and boost growth (Freestone et al., 2007; Lyte and Ernst, 1992; Rooks et al., 2017; Dichtl et al., 2019), we propose that E. lenta uses these molecules as electron acceptors.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Dadh might represent a novel strategy by which gut bacteria take advantage of catecholamines present in the gastrointestinal tract.
claims.source: Thus, Dadh might represent a novel strategy by which gut bacteria take advantage of catecholamines present in the gastrointestinal tract (Eisenhofer et al., 1997; Eisenhofer et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This is a proposal based on the findings and supported by citations on catecholamine levels in the gut.

claims.claim: A working model is proposed in which catechol dehydroxylation is performed by distinct enzymes that are specialized for individual substrates.
claims.source: Further biochemical studies are important for validating the activities of the remaining enzymes, but our preliminary data support a working model in which catechol dehydroxylation is performed by distinct enzymes that are specialized for individual substrates.
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented.

claims.claim: Large numbers of uncharacterized dehydroxylases are encoded within individual Eggerthella and Gordonibacter genomes.
claims.source: We identified large numbers of uncharacterized dehydroxylases encoded within individual Eggerthella and Gordonibacter genomes (Figure 7), hinting at an expansion of this group of enzymes among human gut Actinobacteria.
claims.evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Expansion of enzyme families within specific clades of gut microbes is well-characterized in the context of polysaccharide metabolism.
claims.source: Expansion of enzyme families within specific clades of gut microbes is well-characterized in the context of polysaccharide metabolism. For example, individual human gut Bacteroides strains isolates harbor hundreds of polysaccharide utilization loci but upregulate only a subset of genes in response to distinct substrates (Martens et al., 2011; Rogowski et al., 2015; Ndeh et al., 2017; Larsbrink et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The diversity of catechol dehydroxylases might have evolved in a similar manner to polysaccharide utilization enzymes, providing a biochemical arsenal that enables Actinobacteria to use a range of different electron acceptors.
claims.source: The diversity of catechol dehydroxylases might have evolved in a similar manner, providing a biochemical arsenal that enables Actinobacteria to use a range of different electron acceptors whose availability depends on the diet and/or physiology of the host.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation based on analogy to polysaccharide metabolism.

claims.claim: The study illustrates that the chemical strategies used to enable microbial survival and interactions in the human gut may be relevant to a broad range of species and habitats.
claims.source: In addition to uncovering the diversity of catechol dehydroxylases, our study illustrates that the chemical strategies used to enable microbial survival and interactions in the human gut may be relevant to a broad range of species and habitats.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the distribution of dehydroxylases across diverse organisms and habitats.

claims.claim: The study provides functional evidence for conservation of specific gut microbial metabolic pathways across distinct hosts.
claims.source: While mammalian gut microbiomes have previously been compared in terms of gene content and species composition (Reese et al., 2019; Coelho et al., 2018; Youngblut et al., 2019), our study provides functional evidence for conservation of specific gut microbial metabolic pathways across distinct hosts.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the study and supported by citations.

claims.claim: Gut microbial carbohydrate-degrading enzymes and glycyl radical enzymes are also found in environmental isolates.
claims.source: For example, gut microbial carbohydrate-degrading enzymes and glycyl radical enzymes, which play important roles in degrading diet-derived polysaccharides, amino acids, and osmolytes in the human gut, are also found in environmental isolates (Ndeh et al., 2017; Levin et al., 2017; Craciun and Balskus, 2012; Peck et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Enzyme discovery in the human gut microbiota has implications for improving human health and disease, and for discovering novel catalytic functions and metabolic pathways broadly relevant to microbial life.
claims.source: Enzyme discovery in the human gut microbiota not only has implications for improving human health and disease, but also for discovering novel catalytic functions and metabolic pathways broadly relevant to microbial life.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the broader significance of the work.

claims.claim: The study underscores how enzyme discovery can help to dissect the metabolic diversity of gut microbial strains and communities.
claims.source: More broadly, our study underscores how enzyme discovery can help to dissect the metabolic diversity of gut microbial strains and communities.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claims.claim: Specific catechol dehydroxylases are variably distributed among closely related strains and human gut metagenomes.
claims.source: Although previous studies had linked certain dehydroxylation reactions to individual gut Actinobacteria (Maini Rekdal et al., 2019; Takagaki and Nanjo, 2015; Selma et al., 2014; Bess et al., 2020), we have found that specific catechol dehydroxylases are variably distributed among closely related strains and human gut metagenomes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics and metagenomic data.

claims.claim: These findings reinforce the idea that gut microbial phylogeny is often not predictive of functional capabilities.
claims.source: These findings reinforce the idea that gut microbial phylogeny is often not predictive of functional capabilities (Koppel et al., 2018; Maini Rekdal et al., 2019; Levin et al., 2017; Craciun and Balskus, 2012; Peck et al., 2019; Martínez-del Campo et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: The prevalence of different dehydroxylation reactions among human and animal gut microbiota samples reflected their distribution among individual Actinobacterial strains.
claims.source: Additionally, we noticed that the prevalence of the different dehydroxylation reactions among human and animal gut microbiota samples reflected their distribution among individual Actinobacterial strains, with hydrocaffeic acid metabolism being the most prevalent across all strains and species, and DOPAC dehydroxylation being the least prevalent.
claims.evidence: This is an observation based on comparing strain-level and community-level data.

claims.claim: The strain-level variability in dehydroxylases may be important for metabolism both within humans and other mammalian species.
claims.source: This may suggest that the strain-level variability in dehydroxylases is important for metabolism both within humans and other mammalian species.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between strain-level and community-level metabolism.

claims.claim: The findings provide a framework for linking metabolic transformations performed by complex gut microbial communities to individual strains, genes, and enzymes.
claims.source: Finally, our findings provide a framework for linking metabolic transformations performed by complex gut microbial communities to individual strains, genes, and enzymes.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claims.claim: The functional group-focused approach may greatly increase the efficiency with which we can link metabolic activities to microbial genes and enzymes.
claims.source: This functional group-focused approach may greatly increase the efficiency with which we can link metabolic activities to microbial genes and enzymes.
claims.evidence: This is a proposal about the utility of the approach used in the study.

claims.claim: Related experimental workflows could find broad utility in the discovery of gut microbial enzymes catalyzing other widespread, biologically significant reactions.
claims.source: We envision that related experimental workflows could find broad utility in the discovery of gut microbial enzymes catalyzing other widespread, biologically significant reactions, including reductive metabolism of additional functional groups that are prevalent in diverse molecules encountered by the gut microbiota (Koppel et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a proposal about future applications of the approach and supported by a citation.

results.result: Dadh, a molybdenum-dependent enzyme from E. lenta, specifically dehydroxylates catecholamine neurotransmitters (dopamine and norepinephrine) with a narrow substrate scope requiring the intact catechol moiety.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C20-C23 are supported by enzyme assays (Figure 1C, 1E) showing Dadh metabolizes only dopamine and norepinephrine, with the catechol moiety being absolutely necessary. The substrate specificity is well-documented through systematic testing of dopamine analogs.

results.result: The regulation of dadh is specific for the catecholamine scaffold, with dopamine proposed as the endogenous substrate based on transcriptional induction, enzyme kinetics, and physiological relevance.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 1F) showing specific induction by catecholamines but not by analogs lacking the catechol or having shorter side chains. The proposal that dopamine is the endogenous substrate is well-reasoned based on multiple lines of evidence including enzyme performance and gut dopamine levels.

results.result: Dadh differs mechanistically from 4-HCBR in that it does not require an electron-withdrawing substituent and can tolerate electron-donating hydroxyl groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C28 and C30 are supported by substrate scope data (Figure 1D, 1E) showing Dadh tolerates additional hydroxyl groups (analogs 11-13), contrasting with the known requirements of 4-HCBR. The comparison is appropriately supported by citations.

results.result: A proposed catalytic mechanism for Dadh involves catechol coordination to molybdenum, tautomerization, oxygen atom transfer, and rearomatization, consistent with other bis-MGD enzyme mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C32 present a speculative mechanism (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) based on chemical reasoning and analogy to other molybdenum enzymes. While the proposal is chemically reasonable and consistent with known bis-MGD mechanisms, it lacks direct experimental validation such as crystallographic or spectroscopic evidence.

results.result: Dopamine serves as an alternative electron acceptor for E. lenta, providing a growth advantage in minimal medium lacking other electron acceptors, with the benefit directly tied to dopamine dehydroxylation.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are supported by growth experiments (Figure 2A, 2B) showing dose-dependent growth increase with dopamine in basal medium, specific to metabolizing strains, and blocked by tungstate (which inactivates the molybdenum cofactor). The parallel to reductive dehalogenation provides a reasonable mechanistic framework.

results.result: Dopamine dehydroxylation increases the fitness of metabolizing E. lenta strains in both defined and complex microbial communities, with dopamine promoting growth and enrichment of active dadh variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are supported by competition experiments (Figure 2C), defined community experiments (Figure 2D), and ex vivo human fecal cultures (Figure 2E, 2F) with appropriate statistical tests (p<0.001, p<0.01). The shift from mixed to predominantly active dadh variants provides strong evidence for fitness advantage.

results.result: DOPAC and hydrocaffeic acid are directly dehydroxylated by gut Actinobacteria, representing the first isolation of strains capable of these transformations previously only observed in complex communities.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by LC-MS analysis (Figure 3) confirming production of dehydroxylated metabolites. The novelty claim is appropriately supported by citations to historical literature showing these activities were previously only observed in complex communities.

results.result: Different catechol substrates induce expression of distinct, substrate-specific dehydroxylase enzymes in gut Actinobacteria, as demonstrated by lysate specificity assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are supported by lysate assays (Figure 4A, 4B) showing each lysate quantitatively dehydroxylated only the substrate used for induction. The inducibility was established (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and the specificity pattern supports the hypothesis of distinct enzymes.

results.result: E. lenta uses distinct molybdenum-dependent enzymes (hcdh and cadh) to dehydroxylate hydrocaffeic acid and (+)-catechin, as supported by RNA-seq, tungstate inhibition, and comparative genomics.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are supported by RNA-seq identifying highly upregulated molybdenum-dependent enzymes, tungstate inhibition experiments (Figure 4—figure supplements 2-3), and correlation between gene presence and metabolism across strains (Figure 4C). The evidence converges to support distinct enzymes for different substrates.

results.result: The molybdenum-dependent enzyme C1877_13905 (dodh) in G. pamelaeae is the candidate DOPAC dehydroxylase, supported by RNA-seq and comparative genomics.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by two independent RNA-seq experiments showing >1700-fold induction, correlation between gene presence and DOPAC metabolism (Figure 4C), and sequence similarity to Cldh (45% identity), which dehydroxylates the related lignan dmSECO. The convergent evidence supports the assignment.

results.result: Unlike Eggerthella dehydroxylases, tungstate does not inhibit DOPAC dehydroxylation by G. pamelaeae, possibly because the enzyme can use both molybdenum and tungsten.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by experimental data (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), but C62 is speculative. While the explanation based on analogy to other enzymes is reasonable and cited, it lacks direct experimental validation. Alternative explanations (e.g., different cofactor accessibility) are not excluded.

results.result: Partial purification and proteomics confirmed that Hcdh (Elenta-A2_02815) specifically dehydroxylates hydrocaffeic acid but not other catechols.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C65 are supported by enzyme assays (Figure 4D, 4E) showing quantitative hydrocaffeic acid dehydroxylation and proteomics (Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 2f) confirming Hcdh presence in the active fraction. The substrate specificity matches lysate experiments.

results.result: Catechol dehydroxylases comprise distinct subtypes: E. lenta enzymes are membrane-bound complexes with TAT signal sequences, while G. pamelaeae enzymes are likely soluble complexes with different genomic organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C72 are supported by sequence analysis, genomic context analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 6), and proteomics showing TAT signal cleavage (Figure 4—figure supplement 5). The structural and organizational differences are well-documented, though the membrane-bound vs. soluble distinction is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Catechol dehydroxylases are variably but widely distributed in human gut metagenomes, with prevalence patterns consistent with their distribution among cultured isolates.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74 are supported by analysis of >1800 human gut metagenomes (Figure 5A) showing dadh and hcdh in >70% and >90% of individuals, respectively. The consistency between metagenomic and culture-based data strengthens the findings.

results.result: Catechol dehydroxylation is prevalent but variable in human fecal samples cultured ex vivo, with dodh abundance discriminating DOPAC metabolizers from non-metabolizers and correlating with activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C77 are supported by ex vivo culturing (Figure 5B-D) and qPCR data (Figure 5E, 5F) showing significant discrimination (p<0.001) and correlation (r=0.73, p<0.05) between dodh abundance and DOPAC metabolism. The statistical analyses are appropriate.

results.result: Catechol dehydroxylases form a unique clade within the bis-MGD enzyme family, most closely related to acetylene hydratase and distinct from other characterized family members.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 6) and sequence similarity network analysis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1-2) showing catechol dehydroxylases cluster separately from other bis-MGD enzymes including pyrogallol hydroxytransferase. The clustering does not simply reflect organismal phylogeny.

results.result: Catechol dehydroxylases are present in diverse bacteria and Archaea from various habitats, including soil-dwelling Streptomycetes and anaerobic aromatic compound degraders, likely reflecting catechol substrate availability.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 7) identifying dehydroxylase homologs across diverse organisms and habitats. The distribution is well-documented with appropriate citations, though the inference about substrate availability is reasonable but not directly tested.

results.result: Dehydroxylase homologs contribute to both secondary metabolism (e.g., CC-1065 biosynthesis in Streptomyces) and primary metabolism (e.g., 3,5-DHB degradation in Thauera), representing vast uncharacterized diversity.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by citations to genetic studies showing enzyme essentiality for CC-1065 production and impaired growth on 3,5-DHB in knockout strains. The conclusion about vast diversity is supported by phylogenetic analysis, though most sequences remain functionally uncharacterized.

results.result: Catechol dehydroxylation occurs across gut microbiotas of diverse mammals spanning different diets and phylogenies, with hydrocaffeic acid metabolism being most prevalent.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 are supported by ex vivo culturing experiments with 12 mammalian species (Figure 8) showing variable but widespread catechol dehydroxylation. The authors appropriately note that larger sample sizes are needed for definitive conclusions about substrate-host associations.

results.result: A working model proposes that catechol dehydroxylation is performed by distinct substrate-specific enzymes, with expansion of this enzyme family in gut Actinobacteria potentially providing a biochemical arsenal for using diverse electron acceptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 are supported by the experimental data showing enzyme specificity and genomic diversity (Figure 7). However, C103 is speculative, drawing an analogy to polysaccharide metabolism without direct experimental support. The model is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: The study demonstrates that chemical strategies used in the human gut are relevant to diverse species and habitats, providing functional evidence for conservation of gut microbial metabolic pathways across hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 are supported by the distribution of dehydroxylases across diverse organisms and habitats, and the demonstration of catechol dehydroxylation in multiple mammalian gut microbiotas. The comparison to other enzyme families (carbohydrate-degrading enzymes, glycyl radical enzymes) is appropriately cited.

results.result: Specific catechol dehydroxylases are variably distributed among closely related strains and human gut metagenomes, reinforcing that gut microbial phylogeny is often not predictive of functional capabilities.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by comparative genomics (Figure 4C) and metagenomic data showing variable distribution of specific dehydroxylases. The observation that prevalence patterns in communities reflect strain-level distribution is well-documented, and the conclusion about phylogeny not predicting function is appropriately cited.

results.result: Catechol dehydroxylation is a central but poorly understood gut microbial transformation, with the vast majority of gut microbial metabolic reactions not yet linked to specific enzymes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C11, and C16 establish the knowledge gap addressed by the study. These are appropriately supported by citations and represent accurate statements about the state of the field prior to this work.

results.result: Background claims about the gut microbiota, catechol dehydroxylation, and its substrates establish the biological and chemical context for the study.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C15 provide background information appropriately supported by citations. These establish the importance of gut microbial metabolism, the nature of catechol dehydroxylation, and the biological significance of this transformation.

results.result: Previous work identified Dadh as a molybdenum-dependent enzyme induced >2500-fold by dopamine in E. lenta, predicted to bind bis-MGD cofactor.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C19 summarize previous work by the same authors, appropriately cited. The prediction about bis-MGD binding is based on sequence analysis and is consistent with the experimental evidence presented in the current study.

results.result: The effect of dopamine on E. lenta contrasts with digoxin, which is reduced without impacting growth in the same medium.
results.evaluation: Claim C36 is supported by citation to a previous study. This comparison helps establish the novelty of dopamine serving as an electron acceptor rather than simply being metabolized.

results.result: Among human gut bacteria, only Eggerthella and closely related Actinobacteria have been reported to perform catechol dehydroxylation.
results.evaluation: Claim C45 is appropriately supported by citations to previous literature. This establishes the rationale for focusing the bacterial screen on Actinobacteria.

results.result: Dadh represents the first catecholamine-metabolizing enzyme from a human gut commensal and may represent a novel strategy for using gut catecholamines, contrasting with pathogen strategies.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 are supported by the experimental data and appropriately cited literature on pathogen-catecholamine interactions. The proposal that Dadh represents a novel strategy is reasonable given the demonstrated electron acceptor function, though the full physiological significance remains to be established.

results.result: Expansion of enzyme families within specific gut microbial clades is well-characterized for polysaccharide metabolism.
results.evaluation: Claim C102 is appropriately supported by citations to previous literature on Bacteroides polysaccharide utilization loci. This provides context for interpreting the diversity of catechol dehydroxylases.

results.result: The study provides a framework for linking community-level metabolic transformations to individual strains, genes, and enzymes, with potential broad utility for discovering other gut microbial enzymes.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 describe the methodological contribution of the study. The functional group-focused approach is demonstrated through the work, though claims about future utility (C114-C115) are speculative but reasonable proposals.

results.result: The study underscores how enzyme discovery can help dissect the metabolic diversity of gut microbial strains and communities.
results.evaluation: Claim C108 is a general statement about the significance of the work that is supported by the comprehensive characterization of catechol dehydroxylases from genes to community function.
